title: Where Average Cost Is Lowest
short: Average cost is lowest where it equals marginal cost, and the quotient rule shows why.
trouble: Students set marginal cost to zero to find the lowest average cost.

blocks.html: In Cost Functions and Marginal Cost you saw marginal cost cross average cost at the bottom of the average cost curve. The The Quotient Rule shows that this is not a coincidence of the pictures but a fact about every cost function.
$$AC'(q) = \frac{MC(q) - AC(q)}{q}.$$ So average cost falls while $MC < AC$, rises while $MC > AC$, and is lowest where $MC = AC$. The same holds for average variable cost and $MC$.

By the quotient rule, $$\frac{d}{dq}\left(\frac{C(q)}{q}\right) = \frac{qC'(q) - C(q)}{q^2} = \frac{C'(q) - C(q)/q}{q}.$$ The intuition is the grade-point average: one more unit costing more than the current average pulls the average up, and one costing less pulls it down. At the bottom the marginal unit costs exactly the average. Setting $MC = 0$ finds where total cost is flat, which is a different (and usually meaningless) point.

blocks.name: ec-costcurves
blocks.cap: $MC$ crosses $AVC$ at its minimum ($q = 5$, \$7.50) and $ATC$ at its minimum ($q = 10$, \$20). Drag the marker: to the left of each crossing $MC$ is below the average, to the right above it.

blocks.title: Quadratic cost
blocks.q: $C(q) = 100 + q^2$. Where is average cost lowest, and what is it?
steps: Check: $MC = 2q = 20$ at $q = 10$. Equal, as the rule says.

blocks.title: Average variable cost of a cubic
steps: This minimum is the shutdown price of The Shutdown Rule: below \$7.50 the firm can't cover its variable cost.

blocks.title: With a constant marginal piece
steps: The constant 10 per unit shifts both curves up but does not move the minimum: only the trade-off between spreading the fixed cost (9) and the rising part ($q^2/4$) does.

blocks.html: The bottom of average cost matters twice later in the course: it is the break-even price for a competitive firm (at a lower price it loses money), and with free entry it is where the price settles in the long run (Long-Run Industry Equilibrium).

Setting marginal cost equal to zero to find the lowest average cost. For $C = 100 + q^2$, $MC = 2q = 0$ gives $q = 0$, where average cost is infinite. The minimum of a ratio comes from the derivative of the ratio: set $MC = AC$. Check: at your answer, compute both MC and AC. They must be equal.
